prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on the magic-wavelength principle and its development to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep B015 as a single-part prize for Katori and Ye, and my position is unchanged from round 1 after reading the full exchange. The core is a mechanism I can state in one line: at the magic wavelength the differential light shift of the two clock states cancels, so an ensemble of atoms confined in a lattice, free of Doppler and recoil broadening, becomes a frequency reference. That is a new principle, not only a better version of an old one, and it is the reason the many-atom clock exists at all. Ye's group then showed what the principle allows: control and measurement of each systematic shift (blackbody radiation, hyperpolarisability, collisions) to the 10^-18 range, spin-exchange and many-body physics inside the clock, and gravitational redshift resolved across a sub-millimetre cloud. Because JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and NPL compare clocks that agree, the result is understood and not just claimed. I also accept the chair's point that unanimity of ranking is not merit; my case rests on the principle, the reproduction, and the clean split between originator and perfecter. On timing, I do not think we should wait for the SI second. The physics is already settled, and a redefinition would follow from the prize-worthy work and not validate it. The citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice principle and the 10^-18 regime, and should say nothing about lattice clocks being the only route to that accuracy.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains that this is invention and measurement more than the discovery of a phenomenon, and that Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already recognised the enabling toolbox, with ion clocks as direct competitors. I think the lattice principle answers the first part, but the second part is genuine and the citation has to be careful. Credit is also not perfectly sealed: Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the Al+/Yb+ ion-clock groups contributed, and part of Ye's performance rests on combs and ultrastable cavities built by others. I also see a risk in my own preference: I ranked B015 sixth on my opening ballot and moved to it after reading colleagues' ballots. The reasons I gave hold up on re-reading, but a late move that follows the group is a bias I should name. Finally, if I weigh B015 against the fluctuation theorems I ranked first at opening, the latter are the deeper and more universal statement, but their credit is unsettled and I will not advance a prize whose names I cannot defend.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, concedes that Ye's role partly rests on combs and ultrastable cavities built by others, and asks whether non-AMO members, naming Mehlig and Eriksson, see precision metrology as discovery-like.
responses.response: I accept the challenge directed at me. My low opening rank reflected a preference for universal mechanisms, and I now think the magic-wavelength condition qualifies, since it is a simple, general mechanism that makes a many-body system behave as a single reference. On Ye's reliance on combs and cavities, I would not dilute the credit but the citation should avoid language about frequency combs and credit Ye for the 10^-18 regime and the many-body use of the lattice clock, which is his group's own work. Your Hall-laboratory link is indirect, and since you report no collaboration with Katori or Ye I do not think recusal is required, though it should stay on the record.

responses.point: Lindroth warns that the citation must not suggest lattice clocks alone define the state of the art, since ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) compete at similar accuracy, and notes that this case rests on invention and measurement rather than surprise.
responses.response: I agree with the platform-neutrality point and have changed my citation accordingly: it now credits the invention of the optical lattice clock and the 10^-18 level it reached, with no statement that this platform is the standard. I part from you only mildly on the surprise question. The surprise is not in nature but in the physics of the method, namely that a lattice can be made to leave a clock transition unshifted while holding many atoms, and I think the Committee can say so in its deliberation. I would not add ion-clock names, since the ion work sits with the 2012 prize and would push the configuration over the credit cap.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B014 (Halzen and Karle) as a new window opened by IceCube, but concedes that two names from a collaboration of hundreds is the main weakness, that source identification is thin, and that B015 may be the easier prize to defend.
responses.response: I share your instinct for results that nature hands us, and the diffuse flux is solid. But your own concessions are the ones I would have raised: attribution to two names from a collaboration with AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal and ANTARES predecessors, and a source picture limited to two individually significant objects. As a theorist outside that field I cannot weigh the detector-level claims, so I do not claim to refute your case, only that it is less settled as a prize today than B015. I would be glad to see B014 return in a later year once the source population is clearer, and I would keep it as a strong candidate.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B003 (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue) as a complete theory-experiment arc with more than fifteen years of confirmation, while conceding that Mele, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal are omitted and that B015 is the cleaner attribution case.
responses.response: I agree that B003 is a complete arc, and I said in round 1 that the overlap with the 2016 prize is limited because it concerns real materials with protected edge states. My difficulty is credit. Kane without Mele leaves out the Kane-Mele Z2 classification that is the origin of the idea, and the HgTe experiment followed a proposal by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang that cannot be recognised because Zhang is deceased. Your fallback of Kane and Molenkamp alone is cleaner on attribution, but then Xue's quantum anomalous Hall measurement is a separate achievement left outside. Because you yourself say B015 is the cleaner attribution, I would ask you to treat that as a scientific argument and not only a bureaucratic one. If you cannot support B015, then I would prefer B018 over B003 as a second choice for the topological candidate.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B015 from B039 and says he would consider recusing himself on B039; he also notes that the discovery element of the clock is smaller than the instrument element and calls the judgement close.
responses.response: I agree it is a close judgement, and I would not hide that in the citation wording. Your point about B039 and the 2025 prize is a fair scientific reason to deprioritise circuit QED this year and is not a recusal question for B015, where you report no link. I think your remark that the discovery element is smaller than the instrument element is the right test, and my answer is that an instrument whose principle is new and which measures effects (gravitational redshift inside one cloud, spin-exchange in a clock) that no earlier instrument could resolve is within the prize's purpose. Whether the committee agrees is the real vote.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the magic-wavelength lattice as a new principle distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which is the main point on which a vote could still turn.
Whether the exclusion of Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the ion-clock groups can be defended in the record, and whether the date of the SI second redefinition will change how the prize is read.

How the fluctuation-theorem credit (Jarzynski, Evans, Crooks versus Gallavotti, Cohen, Kurchan, Lebowitz-Spohn, Hatano-Sasa) and the topological-insulator credit (B003 versus B018) will eventually be resolved in a later year.
How much a co-opted member's vote should count, which remains unclear from my role.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. I have no known link to Katori or Ye: they are not among my frequent co-authors, and I have no institutional or collaborative tie to JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE or NPL. My ties are in turbulent aerosols and random-matrix theory, and the Gothenburg link to Chalmers colleagues Johansson and Olsson is institutional only. I note Kroll's Hall-laboratory link and Johansson's possible B039 recusal; neither affects my participation in the B015 deliberation.
